lab_title: VSEPR Theory: Predicting Molecular Geometry from Electron Domains
top_level_objectives: Explain the core principle of VSEPR theory: electron domains arrange to minimize repulsion
Identify and construct the five fundamental electron-domain geometries
Distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry when lone pairs are present
Predict molecular shapes (bent, trigonal pyramidal, seesaw, T-shaped, square planar, square pyramidal) from Lewis structures
Explain why lone pairs cause bond-angle deviations from idealized values
Match VSEPR predictions to real molecules (H2O, NH3, CH4, PF5, SF6, XeF4)

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the transition from flat Lewis structures to three-dimensional electron domain arrangements, setting up the need for VSEPR theory.
key_visuals: A 2D Lewis structure of methane floating in AR space
An animated transformation showing the flat structure lifting into a 3D tetrahedral arrangement
Labels highlighting 'bonding pairs' and 'lone pairs' as distinct electron domains
student_actions: Rotate the 2D Lewis structure to confirm it has no inherent 3D shape
Tap on each electron domain (bond or lone pair) to highlight it
Trigger the animation converting the 2D structure into a 3D electron-domain model

scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate the central VSEPR idea that electron domains push apart from each other until reaching a stable, minimum-energy configuration.
key_visuals: A central atom with a variable number of movable electron-domain spheres attached by flexible bonds
Repulsion force vectors displayed as arrows between domains
A stability meter showing energy decreasing as spheres spread apart
student_actions: Drag electron domains around the central atom to see repulsion forces change in real time
Release the domains and watch them snap into the geometry of minimum repulsion
Repeat with 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 domains to observe each resulting shape

scenes.brief_purpose: Formally present and label the five idealized electron-domain geometries derived from the repulsion-minimization exercise.
key_visuals: Side-by-side 3D models: linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, octahedral
Idealized bond angles labeled on each geometry (180°, 120°, 109.5°, 90°/120°, 90°)
Color-coded domains distinguishing axial vs equatorial positions in trigonal bipyramidal
student_actions: Walk around each 3D geometry model to view it from multiple angles
Tap each geometry to reveal its name and idealized bond angles
Sort a set of domain-count cards (2 through 6) to match each geometry

scenes.brief_purpose: Show how replacing bonding pairs with lone pairs on a fixed electron-domain geometry produces distinct molecular geometries.
key_visuals: A tetrahedral electron-domain framework with one domain converting into a lone pair cloud, revealing trigonal pyramidal ammonia
Further conversion of a second domain into a lone pair, revealing bent water
Similar sequences shown for trigonal bipyramidal (seesaw, T-shaped) and octahedral (square pyramidal, square planar) parents
student_actions: Select which domains become lone pairs on a given parent geometry
Observe the resulting molecular geometry name appear after each conversion
Complete a matching task pairing electron-domain geometry plus lone pair count to the correct molecular shape

scenes.scene_name: Why Lone Pairs Take Up More Space
scenes.brief_purpose: Explain the physical reasoning behind lone-pair vs bonding-pair repulsion strength and its effect on bond angles.
key_visuals: A comparative diagram of a diffuse lone-pair electron cloud versus a tighter bonding-pair cloud
Water molecule with bond angle shown compressing from idealized 109.5° to observed 104.5°
Side-by-side ammonia (107°) and methane (109.5°) angle comparison
student_actions: Slide a comparison tool between lone-pair and bonding-pair cloud sizes to see repulsion strength differences
Adjust a bond-angle dial on the water model to see how deviation relates to lone pair presence
Answer a short prediction question: rank NH3, H2O, and CH4 by expected bond angle

scenes.scene_name: Real Molecules Under the VSEPR Lens
scenes.brief_purpose: Apply the full VSEPR framework to real molecules, letting students verify predictions against known experimental geometries.
key_visuals: A gallery of six 3D molecule models: H2O, NH3, CH4, PF5, SF6, XeF4
Each model displayed with its measured bond angles and geometry name overlay
A toggle switching each model between electron-domain view and molecular (ball-and-stick) view
student_actions: Select each molecule from the gallery and toggle between electron-domain and molecular geometry views
Drag each molecule into a sorting bin labeled with its correct geometry category
Record predicted vs actual bond angles for at least three molecules in a lab notebook widget

scenes.scene_name: Putting It All Together: Predict and Verify
scenes.brief_purpose: Consolidate learning by having students independently derive geometry from a new Lewis structure without guided prompts.
key_visuals: A blank workspace where a new unlabeled Lewis structure (e.g., SF4 or ClF3) appears
Interactive electron-domain construction tools carried over from earlier scenes
A final reveal comparing student-built model to the accepted VSEPR-predicted structure
student_actions: Draw or select the correct number of bonding and lone pair domains for the given molecule
Arrange the domains manually to minimize repulsion before checking against the simulation's auto-solve
Submit a final geometry name and bond-angle estimate for grading feedback
